newsitem.title: RUSSIA: FEATURE - Russia, potato nation, struggles through hardships.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Russia, potato nation, struggles through hardships.

text.p: An extensive survey of the new Russian way of life shows a relatively gloomy picture of a potato-loving nation struggling to survive the difficult transition to a market economy.

The 2,000-page survey "Inside Russia" is the result of a six-month project which questioned nearly 4,000 people living in Russian towns and villages from the Pacific port of Vladivostok to Kaliningrad on the Baltic Sea.

"It is the first such deep and extensive lifestyle survey of Russia. The other new thing is that society has been divided into clusters," said Mark Kotlerenko, commercial director of Britain's Russian Market Research Company.

The clusters -- distinguished by different hopes for the future, different priorities and different amounts of spending power -- include such groups as Potato Growers, living in towns and villages, and the urban Depressed Potato Buyers.

"The authors have put the stress on potatoes, which are Russia's traditional main dietary staple, easy to grow and cheap to buy, because huge population groups are involved in growing or buying them," Kotlerenko said.
Potato Growers, the research company's biggest cluster, account for 26.5 percent of the sample, which would work out at about 39.2 million Russians on a national basis.

Most are office workers who also have small country plots where they grow potatoes and other vegetables. They have found the recent transition hard and painful, but their average income of about $200 a month remains relatively high.
Depressed Potato Buyers, a low-income middle class group, makes up 19.2 percent of respondents -- equivalent to 28.4 million Russians.
Their earnings average just $120 a month and they spend a large proportion of that on basic food. This group is the most pessimistic about their own life and the future of Russia.
The so-called Immobile Villagers made up 16 percent of the survey, comprising poor, ageing and poorly educated individuals whose monthly income is just $50.
OTHER END OF THE SCALE

At the other end of the scale the researchers have identified the Manhattans, a tiny elite of Russians earning at least $400 a month and often much, much more and making up just 3.9 percent of those surveyed. This would work out at 5.8 million people.

The Manhattans own cars, hold credit cards and travel abroad, mainly to the United States and Western Europe, and they shop in expensive Western-style supermarkets. Their standard of living is getting better all the time.
"Had the Soviet Union survived, these individuals would have been the future members of the Politburo, factory chiefs and office leaders," the research survey said.
"When not in the office, Russia's upper management can be seen at the theatre, at the trendy night club or travelling abroad."
The so-called Young Russians -- almost six percent of the sample -- are the up-and-coming elite. They earn at least $440 a month and are Russia's biggest consumers of new cars.
With the exception of the Young Russians, there are no clear age barriers in the groups, but Russians aged 65 and over said life was becoming unbearable and would become much worse.
DIFFERING PERCEPTIONS
"For the 65-plus, 67 percent saw last year as worse, much worse or unbearable. For the coming year...older (people) still expect it to get worse," the survey said.
However most people aged between 16 and 44 in all groups are broadly optimistic.
More than half said life was getting better and they expected it to either improve even more this year or remain the same.

The comments from the young appear more optimistic than those in a survey released by VTsIOM pollsters on March 30 in which two thirds of people questioned said events in Russia were going the wrong way or heading towards a dead-end.
They were asked: "What do you think -- are things in Russia going in the right direction or do you think events are not taking us that way, are leading us towards a dead end?"
Opinion polls are not widely trusted in Russia. But many Russians are disillusioned with wage and pension arrears and with painful economic reforms.
The survey from the Russian Market Research Company showed that Russians were worried about inflation, crime and the environment.

Many richer Russians admitted they had had contacts with the criminal world and about 40 percent of Manhattans said they had been singled out by criminals. But most people said they thought police were more corrupt than criminals.
More than 60 percent of Russians think tax evasion is not a crime and say taxes should be avoided, which is bad news for the Russian government, fighting to raise money for the budget.

Only 18.8 percent say they earn enough to save something. Most would invest their money in real estate, in durable goods or in hard currency, with only a handful of respondents ready to trust the stock market.
Russians like watching television soap operas and quiz shows as well as sports, especially figure skating. Hobbies include sewing and cooking, and many have pets at home.
But some stereotypes hold true. A Russian also enjoys his vodka, preferrably Stolichnaya, and, despite Western influence, likes to listen Soviet-era songs and folk music on the radio.
"The top alcoholic beverage consumed of course is vodka," the survey said.
